sources.name: CFPB, How does compound interest work?

facts.text: Compound interest is interest paid on principal and on accumulated interest.
Example: $1,000 earning 5 percent interest compounded once a year becomes $1,050 after the first year (5 percent of $1,000 is $50) and $1,102.50 after the second year (5 percent of $1,050 is $52.50).

Rule of 72: divide 72 by the interest rate to estimate how many years it takes an investment to double. At a 9 percent rate of return, an investment doubles about every 8 years (72 divided by 9 equals 8).

assumptions.text: Illustration only, computed by us: $1,000 at 7 percent a year, compounded annually for 30 years, grows to about $7,612. This is an example, not a prediction; real returns vary and investments can lose value.
